title: Unit Converter catalog
source: Jeff Jenness's Unit Converter database (conversions.mdb, 2000-2001), with every unit's factor rebuilt against its class's base unit from exact definitions (international foot 0.3048 m, US gallon 231 cubic inches, imperial gallon 4.54609 L, avoirdupois pound 0.45359237 kg, standard gravity 9.80665 m/s2).

units.name: meters
units.definition: The meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: fermis
units.definition: The fermi is a unit of length named for the Italian-born American physicist Enrico Fermi, equal to 1.0 e-15 meters.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: millimeters
units.definition: A millimeter is a unit of length equal to one one-thousandth of a meter.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: centimeters
units.definition: A centimeter is a unit of length equal to one one-hundredth of a meter.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: kilometers
units.definition: A kilometer is a unit of length equal to 1,000 meters.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: angstroms
units.definition: An angstrom is a unit of length named for Swedish scientist Anders Jonas Ångström, equal to 1.0 e-10 meters.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: nanometers
units.definition: A nanometer (or millimicron) is a unit of length equal to 1.0 e-9 meters.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: astronomical units
units.definition: An astronomical unit (AU) is a unit of distance defined as the average distance between the earth and the sun.

units.name: light years
units.definition: A light year is a unit of length defined by the distance that light travels in a year.

units.name: microns
units.definition: A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: micrometers
units.definition: A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: parsecs
units.definition: A parsec is a unit of distance defined as the distance to a star that shows a parallax, or apparent shift in position when viewed from opposite sides of the earth's orbit, of one second of arc. The word parsec is derived by combining the words parallax and second.  This distance is approximately equal to 3.1 e+13 kilometers.

units.name: chains (Gunter)
units.definition: Gunter's (or Surveyor's) chain is a unit of length equal to 66 feet.  Ten square chains equal one acre.

units.name: fathoms
units.definition: A fathom is a unit of length commonly used to measure water or mine depth, and is equal to 6 feet.  The word is Old English, for the outstretched arms, and the fathom is the length they cover; it is now used chiefly for the depth of water.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: feet
units.definition: A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: inches
units.definition: An inch is a unit of length, equal to one one-twelfth of a foot.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: mils
units.definition: A mil is a unit of length, equal to one one-thousandth of an inch or one twelve-thousandth of a foot.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: miles
units.definition: A mile is a unit of length, equal to 5,280 feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.

units.name: miles, nautical
units.definition: A nautical mile is a unit of length, equal to one minute of arc on the earth's surface at the equator.  A nautical mile equals about 1.15 international miles.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.  This International Nautical Mile was defined as exactly 1,852 meters by the First International Extraordinary Hydrographic Conference in Monaco in 1929.

units.name: points
units.definition: A point is a printer's unit of length, where seventy-two points make an inch.

units.name: twips
units.definition: A twip is a unit of length, and is short for "TWenty In a Point", and is therefore equal to one twentieth of a point.  A point is one seventy-second of an inch, and therefore there are 1,440 twips in an inch.

units.name: rods
units.definition: A rod (or perch, lug or pole), is a unit of length equal to 16.5 feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.  The rod originally was defined as the length of the left feet of 16 men lined up heel to toe as they emerged from church.

units.name: yards
units.definition: A yard is a unit of length equal to 3 feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: degrees Fahrenheit
units.definition: The Fahrenheit temperature scale was developed by the German physicist Gabriel Daniel Fahrenheit (1686-1736).  Thirty-two degrees is set at the freezing point of water and 212 degrees is set at the boiling point of water.

units.name: degrees Celsius
units.definition: The Celsius (or Centigrade) temperature scale was developed by the Swedish astronomer and inventor Anders Celsius (1701-1744).  The Celsius scale is essentially identical to the Centigrade scale, in which zero degrees is set at the freezing point of water and 100 degrees is set at the boiling point of water.  In 1954 the General Conference on Weights and Measures based the scale, through the kelvin, on the triple point of water (the temperature at which water can exist as a solid, a liquid and a gas), set at 273.16 kelvins, or 0.01 degrees Celsius.  Since 2019 the kelvin, and with it the Celsius scale, has been defined by a fixed value of the Boltzmann constant.

units.name: Kelvin
units.definition: The Kelvin temperature scale was developed by the Scottish physicist William Thomson, Baron Kelvin (1824-1907), who described it in 1848.  Zero degrees is set at absolute zero (-273.15 Celsius) and the degree intervals correspond to those of the Celsius (or Centigrade) scale.

units.name: degrees Rankine
units.definition: The Rankine temperature scale was developed by the British engineer and physicist William J. M. Rankine (1820-1872).  Zero degrees is set at absolute zero (-459.67 Fahrenheit) and the degree intervals correspond to those of the Fahrenheit scale.

units.name: feet (US Survey)
units.definition: The Survey foot is a unit of length defined by the US Metric Law of 1893, equal to (1200/3937) of a meter.  The definition of a foot was changed in 1959 to be equal to exactly 0.3048 meters, and this modern definition (sometimes called the "international foot") is used much more often today. The U.S. survey foot was retired by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the National Geodetic Survey at the end of 2022; since then, U.S. measurements use the international foot of exactly 0.3048 meter. This unit is kept for older surveys and records.

units.name: furlongs
units.definition: A furlong is a unit of distance equal to one eighth of a mile or 660 feet.  The word is derived from the length of a furrow in medieval British farming, or "furrow-long."

units.name: sq feet
units.definition: A square foot is a unit of area equal to 144 square inches.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: sq feet (Survey)
units.definition: A square survey foot is a unit of area equal to .999996 square feet.  The Survey foot is a unit of length defined by the US Metric Law of 1893, equal to (1200/3937) meters.  The definition of a foot was changed in 1959 to be equal to exactly 0.3048 meters, and this modern definition (sometimes called the "international foot") is used much more often today. The U.S. survey foot was retired by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the National Geodetic Survey at the end of 2022; since then, U.S. measurements use the international foot of exactly 0.3048 meter. This unit is kept for older surveys and records.

units.name: acres
units.definition: An acre is a unit of area equal to 10 square chains or 43,560 square feet.  A chain (Gunter's or Surveyor's) is a unit of length equal to 66 feet.  An acre was originally defined as the amount of land that a yoke of oxen could plough in a day, and eventually redefined as an area equal to "40 poles long by 4 broad," or 32 furrow-lengths.

units.name: ares
units.definition: An are is an area equal to 100 square meters, or a square measuring 10 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: sq kilometers
units.definition: A square kilometer is a unit of area equal to a square 1,000 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: hectares
units.definition: A hectare is a unit of area equal to a square 100 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: sq meters
units.definition: A square meter is a unit of area equal to a square one meter on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: sq millimeters
units.definition: A square millimeter is a unit of area equal to a square .001 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: sq centimeters
units.definition: A square centimeter is a unit of area equal to a square .01 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: sq micrometers
units.definition: A square micrometer (or square micron) is a unit of area equal to a square 1.0 e-6 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: sq chains (Gunter)
units.definition: A square chain (Gunter's) is a unit of area equal to one one-tenth of an acre.  A Gunter's (or Surveyor's) chain is a unit of length equal to 66 feet.

units.name: sq inches
units.definition: A square inch is a unit of area equal to a square one one-twelfth of a foot on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: sq mils
units.definition: A square mil is a unit of area equal to a square one one-thousandth of an inch, or one twelve-thousandth of a foot, on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: sq miles
units.definition: A square mile is a unit of area equal to a square 5,280 feet on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.

units.name: sq yards
units.definition: A square yard is a unit of area equal to a square 3 feet on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: sq rods
units.definition: A square rod is a unit of area equal to a square 16.5 feet on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.  The rod originally was defined as the length of the left feet of 16 men lined up heel to toe as they emerged from church.

units.name: sq twips
units.definition: A square twip is a unit of area equal to a square 1/17,280 feet on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.  A twip is a unit of length, and is short for "TWenty In a Point", and is therefore equal to one twentieth of a point.  A point is one seventy-second of an inch, and therefore there are 1,440 twips in an inch.

units.name: sq points
units.definition: A square point is a unit of area equal to a square 1/72 inches, or 1/864 feet, on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: sq angstroms
units.definition: A square angstrom is a very small unit of area equal to a square 1.0 e-10 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: sq nanometers
units.definition: A square nanometer (or square millimicron) is a very small unit of area equal to a square 1.0 e-9 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: sq fermis
units.definition: A square fermi is a very small unit of area equal to a square 1.0 e-15 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: sq microns
units.definition: A square micron (or square micrometer) is a very small unit of area equal to a square 1.0 e-6 meters on a side.  A meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: gallons (US fluid)
units.definition: A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: acre-feet
units.definition: An acre-foot is a unit of volume equal to the amount of fluid it would take to cover one acre to a depth of one foot.  An acre is 43,560 square feet so an acre-foot contains 43,560 cubic feet, usually of water.

units.name: barrels (US fluid)
units.definition: A barrel is a unit of volume or capacity.  There are several types of barrels, each reflecting different fluids or solids they carry.  The US fluid barrel contains 31.5 US liquid gallons.

units.name: barrels (US petro)
units.definition: A barrel is a unit of volume or capacity.  There are several types of barrels, each reflecting different fluids or solids they carry.  A petroleum barrel carries 42 gallons of a petroleum product.

units.name: bushels (US level)
units.definition: A US level bushel is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 32 dry quarts.  It is equivalent to the Winchester bushel of 2,150.42 cubic inches, much used in England from the time of Henry VIII until the imperial bushel was legally established in 1826.

units.name: cu. feet
units.definition: A cubic foot is a unit of volume equal to a cube measuring 1 foot on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: cu. inches
units.definition: A cubic inch is a unit of volume equal to a cube measuring 1 inch on a side.  An inch is a unit of length, equal to one one-twelfth of a foot.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: cu. yards
units.definition: A cubic yard is a unit of volume equal to a cube measuring 3 feet on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: gallons (Brit)
units.definition: A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is a unit of volume defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: gallons (US dry)
units.definition: A dry gallon is a unit of volume or capacity.  US dry gallons are intended for fruits, vegetables and other dry commodities, and are equivalent to about 1.16 liquid gallons.

units.name: gills (US)
units.definition: A gill is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 1/4 of a pint, or 1/32 of a US liquid gallon.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: minims (US)
units.definition: A US minim is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 1/60 of a fluid dram (fluidram), or 1/61,440 of a US fluid gallon.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: ounces (US fluid)
units.definition: A US fluid ounce is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 1/128 of a US liquid gallon.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.  The abbreviation of 'ounce' is 'oz', which derives from the Italian word 'onza', referring to the name of a Spanish and Sicilian coin.

units.name: pints (US fluid)
units.definition: A US fluid pint is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 1/8 of a US liquid gallon.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: quarts (US fluid)
units.definition: A US fluid quart is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 1/4 of a US liquid gallon.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: fluidrams
units.definition: A fluidram (or fluid dram) is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 1/1024 of a US liquid gallon.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: cu. mils
units.definition: A cubic mil is a small unit of volume equal to a cube measuring one mil on a side.  A mil is a unit of length, equal to one one-thousandth of an inch or one twelve-thousandth of a foot.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: teaspoons
units.definition: A teaspoon is a unit of volume or capacity equal to one and one-third fluid drams, or 1/768 of a US liquid gallon.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: tablespoons
units.definition: A tablespoon is a unit of volume or capacity equal to three teaspoons, or 1/256 of a US liquid gallon.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: liters
units.definition: A liter (or litre) is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter, although according to the Oxford English Dictionary (citing the Physics Bull. Feb. 58/2, 1969),  "It was a regrettable international decision in 1964 which reinstated the name litre for a cubic decimetre".  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: cu. centimeters
units.definition: A cubic centimeter is a unit of volume equal to a cube measuring one one-hundredth of a meter on a side.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: cu. meters
units.definition: A cubic meter is a unit of volume equal to a cube measuring one meter on a side.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: hogsheads
units.definition: A unit of volume or capacity equal to 63 US liquid gallons.  The term dates from the 14th century.  Hogsheads were also used for dry goods such as tobacco and sugar, a use now chiefly historical.

units.name: bushels (Brit)
units.definition: A British bushel is a unit of volume equal to 8 British (or Imperial) gallons.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: drams (US fluid)
units.definition: A fluid dram (or fluidram) is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 1/1024 of a US liquid gallon.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: gills (Brit)
units.definition: A British gill is a unit of volume equal to 1/32 of a British (or Imperial) gallon.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: minims (Brit)
units.definition: A British minim is a unit of volume equal to 1/76,800 of a British (or Imperial) gallon.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: ounces (Brit fl)
units.definition: A British fluid ounce is a unit of volume equal to 1/160 of a British (or Imperial) gallon.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.  The abbreviation of 'ounce' is 'oz', which derives from the Italian word 'onza', referring to the name of a Spanish and Sicilian coin.

units.name: pecks (Brit)
units.definition: A British peck is a unit of volume equal to 2 British (or Imperial) gallons.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: pecks (US)
units.definition: A US peck is a unit of volume equal to 2 US dry gallons.  US dry gallons are intended for fruits, vegetables and other dry commodities, and are equivalent to about 1.16 liquid gallons.

units.name: cu. feet (Survey)
units.definition: A Cubic Survey foot is a unit of volume equal to a cube measuring one survey foot on a side.  The Survey foot is a unit of length defined by the US Metric Law of 1893, equal to (1200/3937) meters.  The definition of a foot was changed in 1959 to be equal to exactly 0.3048 meters, and this modern definition (sometimes called the "international foot") is used much more often today. The U.S. survey foot was retired by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the National Geodetic Survey at the end of 2022; since then, U.S. measurements use the international foot of exactly 0.3048 meter. This unit is kept for older surveys and records.

units.name: pints (Brit)
units.definition: A British pint is a unit of volume equal to 1/8 British (or Imperial) gallons.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: pints (US dry)
units.definition: A US dry pint is a unit of volume or capacity slightly larger than the US liquid pint.  US dry pints are intended for fruits, vegetables and other dry commodities.

units.name: quarts (Brit)
units.definition: A British quart is a unit of volume equal to 1/4 British (or Imperial) gallons.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: quarts (US dry)
units.definition: A US dry quart is a unit of volume or capacity slightly larger than the US liquid quart.  US dry quarts are intended for fruits, vegetables and other dry commodities.

units.name: cu. millimeters
units.definition: A cubic millimeter is a unit of volume equal to a cube one one-thousandth of a meter on a side.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: hours
units.definition: An hour is a unit of time defined as one twenty-fourth of a day.  A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

units.name: minutes
units.definition: A minute is a unit of time defined as one sixtieth of an hour, or 1/1440 of a day.  A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

units.name: seconds
units.definition: A second is a unit of time defined as one sixtieth of a minute.  A minute is a unit of time defined as one sixtieth of an hour, or 1/1440 of a day.  A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

units.name: days
units.definition: A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

units.name: years
units.definition: A year is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete rotation around the sun.  In common usage, it refers to the length of time equal to 365 days.

units.name: hours (sidereal)
units.definition: A sidereal hour is a unit of time defined as one twenty-fourth of a sidereal day.  A sidereal day is defined as the time it takes for the earth to make one complete rotation relative to some star other than the sun.

units.name: minutes (sidereal)
units.definition: A sidereal minute is a unit of time defined as one sixtieth of a sidereal hour, or 1/1440 of a sidereal day.  A sidereal day is defined as the time it takes for the earth to make one complete rotation relative to some star other than the sun.

units.name: seconds (sidereal)
units.definition: A sidereal second is a unit of time defined as one sixtieth of a sidereal minute.  A sidereal minute is defined as one sixtieth of a sidereal hour, or 1/1440 of a sidereal day.  A sidereal day is defined as the time it takes for the earth to make one complete rotation relative to some star other than the sun.

units.name: days (sidereal)
units.definition: A sidereal day is a unit of time defined as the time it takes for the earth to make one complete rotation relative to some star other than the sun.

units.name: years (sidereal)
units.definition: A sidereal year is a unit of time defined as the time elapsing between a solar eclipse of some given star and the next solar eclipse of that star.  The sidereal year lasts for 365 days, 6 hours,  9 minutes and 9.54 seconds

units.name: years (tropical)
units.definition: A tropical (or astronomical) year is a unit of time defined as the time elapsing from the appearance of the sun on one of the Tropics, generally at the vernal equinox, until its return to the same place.  The tropical year lasts for 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes and 46 seconds

units.name: shakes
units.definition: A shake is a unit of time defined as one one-hundred-millionth of a second, or 10 nanoseconds.  A second is a unit of time defined as one sixtieth of a minute.  A minute is a unit of time defined as one sixtieth of an hour, or 1/1440 of a day.  A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

units.name: nanoseconds
units.definition: A nanosecond is a unit of time defined as one billionth of a second.  A second is a unit of time defined as one sixtieth of a minute.  A minute is a unit of time defined as one sixtieth of an hour, or 1/1440 of a day.  A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

units.name: barrels (Brit fluid)
units.definition: A barrel is a unit of volume or capacity.  There are several types of barrels, each reflecting different fluids or solids they carry.  A British (or Imperial) barrel holds 36 British gallons, and British liquid barrels hold the same as British dry barrels.

units.name: grams
units.definition: A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: drams (apoth)
units.definition: An apothecaries' dram is a unit of mass equal to 60 grains or 1/8 of an apothecaries' ounce.  It's equal in weight to the troy dram.  Apothecaries' measures originated with early European shopkeepers and pharmacists and are based around the "grain."

units.name: drams (troy)
units.definition: A troy dram is a unit of mass equal to 60 grains or 1/8 of an troy ounce.  It's equal in weight to the apothecaries' dram and generally used for weighing precious metals or apothecaries' drugs.  Troy measurements probably descend from Medieval trade fairs held in the French town of Troyes, in the 12th and 13th centuries.

units.name: drams (avdp)
units.definition: A dram (or avoirdupois dram) is a unit of weight equal to one one-sixteenth of an ounce.  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: dynes
units.definition: A dyne is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second system equal to the force that would give a free mass of one gram an acceleration of one centimeter per second squared.  This force translates to a weight of about .001 grams on the surface of the earth.

units.name: grains
units.definition: A grain is a small unit of weight equal to 0.065 gram, or 1/7,000 pound avoirdupois. The grain is one of the earliest units of common measure, and is a uniform unit in the avoirdupois, apothecaries', and troy systems. The defined weight of the ancient grain varied from culture to culture, but was generally defined as the weight of a designated number of dry wheat (or other edible grain) kernels taken from the middle of the ear.

units.name: hundredweights (long)
units.definition: The hundredweight is a unit of weight dating back to the 16th century.  The long hundredweight (or British hundredweight) is equal to 112 pounds.

units.name: hundredweights (short)
units.definition: The hundredweight is a unit of weight dating back to the 16th century.  The hundredweight (or short hundredweight) is equal to 100 pounds.

units.name: ounces (apoth)
units.definition: An apothecaries' ounce is a unit of apothecaries' weight equal to 480 grains.  It's equal in weight to the troy ounce.  Apothecaries' measures originated with early European shopkeepers and pharmacists and are based around the "grain."  The abbreviation of 'ounce' is 'oz', which derives from the Italian word 'onza', referring to the name of a Spanish and Sicilian coin.

units.name: ounces (troy)
units.definition: A troy ounce is a unit of weight, equal to the apothecaries' ounce and generally used for weighing precious metals or apothecaries' drugs.  Troy measurements probably descend from Medieval trade fairs held in the French town of Troyes, in the 12th and 13th centuries.  The abbreviation of 'ounce' is 'oz', which derives from the Italian word 'onza', referring to the name of a Spanish and Sicilian coin.

units.name: ounces (avdp)
units.definition: An ounce (or avoirdupois ounce) is a unit of weight equal to one one-sixteenth of a pound.  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.  The abbreviation of 'ounce' is 'oz', which derives from the Italian word 'onza', referring to the name of a Spanish and Sicilian coin.

units.name: pennyweights
units.definition: A pennyweight is a unit of weight equal to 24 grains.  A grain is a small unit of weight equal to 0.065 gram, or 1/7,000 pound avoirdupois. The grain is one of the earliest units of common measure, and is a uniform unit in the avoirdupois, apothecaries', and troy systems. The defined weight of the ancient grain varied from culture to culture, but was generally defined as the weight of a designated number of dry wheat (or other edible grain) kernels taken from the middle of the ear.

units.name: poundals
units.definition: A poundal is a unit of force in the foot-pound-second system, and is a unit of force equal to the force that would give a free mass of one pound an acceleration of one foot per second squared.  This force is equal to a weight of .031 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: quarters (Brit long)
units.definition: A British long quarter is a unit of weight equal to 28 pounds, or one quarter of a long hundredweight.  A pound (or avoirdupois pound) is a unit of weight.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."

units.name: pounds (apoth)
units.definition: An apothecaries' (or Troy) pound is a unit of apothecaries' weight equal to 5,760 grains.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  Apothecaries' measures originated with early European shopkeepers and pharmacists and are based around the "grain."

units.name: pounds (troy)
units.definition: A troy pound is a unit of weight, equal to the apothecaries' pound and generally used for weighing precious metals or apothecaries' drugs.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  Troy measurements probably descend from Medieval trade fairs held in the French town of Troyes, in the 12th and 13th centuries.

units.name: pounds (avdp)
units.definition: A pound (or avoirdupois pound) is a unit of weight.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: scruples (apoth)
units.definition: An apothecaries' scruple is a unit of apothecaries' weight equal to twenty grains.  Apothecaries' measures originated with early European shopkeepers and pharmacists and are based around the "grain."  An apothecaries' scruple equals 1/288 of an apothecaries' pound.

units.name: slugs
units.definition: A slug is the gravitational unit of mass in the foot-pound-second system to which a pound force can impart an acceleration of one foot per second squared and which is equal to the mass of an object weighing 32.174 pounds.

units.name: tons (long)
units.definition: A long ton is a British unit of weight equal to 2,240 pounds.  The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: tons
units.definition: A ton is a unit of weight equal to 2,000 pounds.  The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: tonnes
units.definition: A tonne (or metric ton) is a unit of weight equal to 1,000 kilograms.  The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: kilograms
units.definition: A kilogram is a unit of mass equal to 1,000 grams.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: myriagrams
units.definition: A myriagram is a unit of mass equal to 10,000 grams.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: tons (metric)
units.definition: A metric ton (or tonne) is a unit of weight equal to 1,000 kilograms.  The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: quarters (US long)
units.definition: A US long quarter is a unit of weight equal to 560 pounds, or one quarter of a long ton.  A pound (or avoirdupois pound) is a unit of weight.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."

units.name: noggins
units.definition: A noggin is a small unit of volume usually used to measure ale or liquor.  It's a British unit equal to one British gill, or one-fourth of a British pint.

units.name: milliliters
units.definition: A milliliter is a unit of volume equal to 0.001 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: carats (metric)
units.definition: A carat is a unit of weight for diamonds and other precious gems.  The metric carat was standardized in 1913 at 200 milligrams.  The carat weight was originally based on the weight of grains or leguminous seeds.

units.name: carats (1877)
units.definition: A carat is a unit of weight for diamonds and other precious gems.  The 1877 carat weighed 205.3 milligrams.  The metric carat was standardized in 1913 at 200 milligrams.  The carat weight was originally based on the weight of grains or leguminous seeds.

units.name: milligrams
units.definition: A milligram is a unit of mass equal to one one-thousandth of a gram.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: centigrams
units.definition: A centigram is a unit of mass equal to one one-hundredth of a gram.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: centals
units.definition: A cental is a unit of weight equal to 100 pounds, or one hundredweight.  A pound (or avoirdupois pound) is a unit of weight.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: centares
units.definition: A centare is a unit of area equal to 1/100 of an are, or 1 square meter.  The meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: decigrams
units.definition: A decigram is a unit of mass equal to one tenth of a gram.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: dekagrams
units.definition: A dekagram is a unit of mass equal to ten grams.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: hectograms
units.definition: A hectogram is a unit of mass equal to 100 grams.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: kiloliters
units.definition: A kiloliter is a unit of volume equal to 1,000 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: hectoliters
units.definition: A hectoliter is a unit of volume equal to 100 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: dekaliters
units.definition: A dekaliter is a unit of volume equal to 10 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: deciliters
units.definition: A deciliter is a unit of volume equal to 0.1 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: centiliters
units.definition: A centiliter is a unit of volume equal to 0.01 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: paces
units.definition: A pace is a unit of length defined as 2.5 feet, although in practice people often count their own step length (pace) and so a "pace" varies from person to person.  In these cases, a person will measure the length of their pace, then count their paces as they walk, then convert the number of paces to the proper measurement units.

units.name: palms
units.definition: A palm is a unit of length equal to one fourth of a foot, or three inches.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: hands
units.definition: A hand is a unit of length equal to one third of a foot, or four inches.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.  The hand is currently used mainly to measure the height of horses.

units.name: cubits
units.definition: A cubit is an ancient unit of length that was based on the length of the arm from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. In some cultures it was as long as 21 inches, but in most cases it was equal to 18 inches, or 1.5 feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: board feet
units.definition: A board foot is a unit of volume equal to 144 cubic inches.  It is usually applied to wood, such that a board that is 6 inches wide, 24 inches long and 1 inch thick would comprise one board foot.

units.name: acre-inches
units.definition: An acre-inch is a unit of volume equal to the amount of fluid it would take to cover one acre to a depth of one inch.  An acre is 43,560 square feet, so an acre-inch would equal 43,560/12, or 3,630 cubic feet of fluid (usually water).

units.name: decimeters
units.definition: A decimeter is a unit of length equal to one one-tenth of a meter.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: dekameters
units.definition: A dekameter is a unit of length equal to 10 meters.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: hectometers
units.definition: A hectometer is a unit of length equal to 100 meters.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: bolts of cloth
units.definition: A bolt of cloth is a linear measure equal to 120 linear feet of cloth.

units.name: cords
units.definition: A cord is a unit of volume equal to 128 cubic feet.  It is usually applied to volumes of wood, such as a "cord of firewood".  The term 'cord' is probably derived from an early way to measure the stack of wood, by stretching a cord of fixed length around it.

units.name: cu. decimeters
units.definition: A cubic decimeter is a unit of volume equal to a cube 0.1 meters on a side.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: cu. nanometers
units.definition: A cubic nanometer is a small unit of volume equal to a cube measuring 1.0 e-9 meters on a side.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: cu. dekameters
units.definition: A cubic dekameter is a unit of volume equal to a cube 10 meters on a side.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: cu. hectometers
units.definition: A cubic hectometer is a unit of volume equal to a cube 100 meters on a side.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: cu. kilometers
units.definition: A cubic kilometer is a unit of volume equal to a cube 1,000 meters on a side.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: cu. miles
units.definition: A cubic mile is a unit of volume equal to a cube 5,280 feet on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.

units.name: gigameters
units.definition: A gigameter is a unit of length equal to 1.0 e+9 meters.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: geepounds
units.definition: A geepound is a unit of mass equal to a slug.  A slug is the gravitational unit of mass in the foot-pound-second system to which a pound force can impart an acceleration of one foot per second squared and which is equal to the mass of an object weighing a little over 32 pounds.

units.name: spans
units.definition: A span is a unit of length equal to 3/4 of a foot or 9 inches.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: butts
units.definition: A butt is a unit of capacity measuring 126 gallons, used for measuring wine or ale.

units.name: leagues (Brit)
units.definition: The British nautical league is a unit of length equal to 18,240 feet or about 3.45 miles.   A mile is a unit of length, equal to 5,280 feet.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.  In the late 18th century the league also came to be the distance a cannon shot could be fired at menacing ships offshore.  This resulted in the 3-mile offshore territorial limit.

units.name: leagues (Int)
units.definition: The international nautical league is a unit of length equal to about 3.45 miles.   A mile is a unit of length, equal to 5,280 feet.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.  In the late 18th century the league also came to be the distance a cannon shot could be fired at menacing ships offshore.  This resulted in the 3-mile offshore territorial limit. Three international nautical miles of 1,852 meters each: 5,556 meters exactly.

units.name: leagues (statute)
units.definition: A statute league (or land league) is a unit of length equal to 3 miles.  A mile is a unit of length, equal to 5,280 feet.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.  In the late 18th century the league also came to be the distance a cannon shot could be fired at menacing ships offshore. This resulted in the 3-mile offshore territorial limit.

units.name: pottles (Brit)
units.definition: A British pottle is a unit of volume equal to 2 British quarts or 0.5 British gallons.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is a unit of volume defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: quintals
units.definition: A quintal is a unit of mass equal to 100 kilograms or 100,000 grams.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: quarterns (Brit dry)
units.definition: A British dry quartern is a unit of volume equal to a quarter of a British peck or a half of a British gallon.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is a unit of volume defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: quarterns (Brit fl)
units.definition: A British fluid quartern is a unit of volume equal to one quarter of a British pint, or 1/32 of a British gallon.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is a unit of volume defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: tons (register)
units.definition: A register ton a unit of volume equal to 100 cubic feet.    The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: perches
units.definition: A perch (or rod, lug or pole), is a unit of length equal to 16.5 feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.  The rod originally was defined as the length of the left feet of 16 men lined up heel to toe as they emerged from church.

units.name: roods (Brit)
units.definition: A rood is an old English unit of area equal to 40 square rods, or 1/4 of an acre, or 10,890 square feet.

units.name: ropes (Brit)
units.definition: A rope is a British unit of length equal to 20 feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: cable lengths
units.definition: A cable length is a unit of length equal to 720 feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: seams (Brit)
units.definition: A British seam is a unit of volume equal to 8 British bushels.  A British bushel is a unit of volume equal to 8 British (or Imperial) gallons.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: skeins
units.definition: A skein is a unit of length equal to 360 feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: steres
units.definition: A stere is a unit of volume equal to one cubic meter.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: stones (Brit)
units.definition: A stone is a British unit of weight equal to 14 pounds.  A pound (or avoirdupois pound) is a unit of weight.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: sections
units.definition: A section is a unit of area used in US land surveys, equal to one square mile.  There are 36 sections in a township, and each section is numbered according to it's position in the township.

units.name: townships
units.definition: A township is a unit of area used in US land surveys, and is a square measuring 6 miles on a side or 36 square miles total.  The township is broken down into 36 sections of one square mile each, numbered 1 through 36 depending on their location.

units.name: weys (Brit)
units.definition: A wey is a British unit of mass equal to 252 pounds (avdp).  A pound (or avoirdupois pound) is a unit of weight.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: newtons
units.definition: A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  This force is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: quarters (Brit short)
units.definition: A British long quarter is a unit of weight equal to 25 pounds, or one quarter of a short hundredweight.  A pound (or avoirdupois pound) is a unit of weight.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."

units.name: quarters (US short)
units.definition: A US short quarter is a unit of weight equal to 500 pounds, or one quarter of a ton.  A pound (or avoirdupois pound) is a unit of weight.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."

units.name: tuns
units.definition: A tun is a unit of volume, especially referring to a wine cask, holding 252 wine gallons.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: nanograms
units.definition: A kilogram is a small unit of mass equal to 1.0 e-9 grams.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: myriameters
units.definition: A myriameter is a unit of length equal to 10,000 meters.  A meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: drachms (Brit fl)
units.definition: A drachm is another spelling for "dram", a small unit of volume.  A dram is a little less than a teaspoon.

units.name: firkins (Brit)
units.definition: A firkin is a unit of volume first recorded in the 15th century, apparently from a Middle Dutch diminutive of vierde, "fourth."  A firkin equals about one fourth of a barrel.

units.name: firkins (US)
units.definition: A firkin is a unit of volume first recorded in the 15th century, apparently from a Middle Dutch diminutive of vierde, "fourth."  A firkin equals about one fourth of a barrel.

units.name: bags (Brit)
units.definition: A British bag is a unit of volume equal to 3 British bushels.  A British bushel is equal to 8 British (or Imperial) gallons.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: puncheons (Brit)
units.definition: A puncheon is a unit of volume probably originating around the 15th century, referring to a wine or beer cask.

units.name: sq perches
units.definition: A square perch is a unit of area equal to a square measuring one perch, or 16.5 feet, on a side.  A perch is a unit of length equal to a rod, or 16.5 feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.  The rod originally was defined as the length of the left feet of 16 men lined up heel to toe as they emerged from church.

units.name: perches (masonry)
units.definition: A perch of masonry is a unit of volume used to measure stone or masonry, equal to 16.5 ft x 1.5 ft x 1 ft, or 24.75 cubic feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: rods (Brit vol)
units.definition: A British volumetric rod is a unit of volume equal to 1,000 cubic feet.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: quarters (Brit. lin)
units.definition: A British linear quarter is a unit of length equal to one-quarter of a yard, or three-quarters of a foot, or 9 inches.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: links (Gunter)
units.definition: A Gunter's link is a unit of length equal to one one-hundredth of a Gunter's chain, or 0.66 feet.  A Gunter's (or Surveyor's) chain is a unit of length equal to 66 feet.  Ten square chains equal one acre.

units.name: links (Ramsden)
units.definition: A Ramsden's link is a unit of length equal to one one-hundredth of a Ramsden's chain, or 1 foot.  A Ramsden's (or Engineer's) chain is a unit of length equal to 100 feet.

units.name: chains (Ramsden)
units.definition: A Ramsden's (or Engineer's) chain is a unit of length equal to 100 feet.

units.name: sq chains (Ramsden)
units.definition: A square chain (Ramsden's) is a unit of area equal to 10,000 square feet.  A Ramsden's (or Engineer's) chain is a unit of length equal to 100 feet.

units.name: scruples (Brit fl)
units.definition: A British fluid scruple is a British unit of volume equal to 20 British minims.

units.name: leap years
units.definition: A leap year is a year with an extra day in it (February 29), generally occurring every 4 years EXCEPT when the year ends in 00, UNLESS that century change year is divisible by four hundred.

units.name: lunar months
units.definition: A lunar month is a unit of time equal to the time for the moon to complete a full cycle, approximately equal to 29.5 days.

units.name: weeks
units.definition: A week is a unit of time equal to seven days.  A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

units.name: miles/hr
units.definition: Miles per hour is a unit of velocity reflecting how many miles something moves in a hour.  A mile is a unit of length, equal to 5,280 feet.

units.name: feet/hr
units.definition: Feet per hour is a unit of velocity reflecting how many feet something moves in a hour.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: feet/min
units.definition: Feet per minute is a unit of velocity reflecting how many feet something moves in a minute.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: feet/second
units.definition: Feet per second is a unit of velocity reflecting how many feet something moves in a second.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: miles/min

units.name: degrees Réaumur

units.name: cu. astro. units

units.name: cu. light years

units.name: feet dbh

units.name: inches dbh

units.name: feet (circumf.)

units.name: years (astro.)
units.definition: An astronomical (or tropical) year is defined as the time elapsing from the appearance of the sun on one of the Tropics, generally at the vernal equinox, until its return to the same place.  The tropical year lasts for 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes and 46 seconds

units.name: years (anom.)
units.definition: An anomalistic year is defined as the time it takes for the earth to make one complete rotation around the sun.  An anomalistic year lasts for 365 days, 6 hours, 13 minutes and 53.1 seconds

units.name: deciseconds
units.definition: A decisecond is a unit of time defined as one tenth of a second.  A second is defined as one sixtieth of a minute.  A minute is one sixtieth of an hour, or 1/1440 of a day.  A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

units.name: centiseconds
units.definition: A centisecond is a unit of time defined as one one-hundredth of a second.  A second is defined as one sixtieth of a minute.  A minute is one sixtieth of an hour, or 1/1440 of a day.  A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

A minute is one sixtieth of an hour, or 1/1440 of a day.  A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.
