A day is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete revolution relative to some extraterrestrial point of reference, in this case the sun.

units.name: centuries (sid.)
units.definition: A sidereal century is a unit of time defined as 100 sidereal years.  A sidereal year is a unit of time defined as the time elapsing between a solar eclipse of some given star and the next solar eclipse of that star.  The sidereal year lasts for 365 days, 6 hours,  9 minutes and 9.54 seconds

units.name: centuries (anom.)
units.definition: An anomalistic century is a unit of time defined as 100 anomalistic years.  An anomalistic year is defined as the time it takes for the earth to make one complete rotation around the sun.  An anomalistic year lasts for 365 days, 6 hours, 13 minutes and 53.1 seconds

units.name: eons
units.definition: An eon (or aeon) is a unit of time equal to 1 billion years.  It is also commonly used to refer to specific geologic time spans of variable length in earth's history.  A year is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete rotation around the sun.  In common usage, it refers to the length of time equal to 365 days.

units.name: centuries (cal.)
units.definition: A century (calendar) is a unit of time equal to 100 years; in this case 76 years plus 24 leap years.  A year is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete rotation around the sun.  In common usage, it refers to the length of time equal to 365 days.  A leap year is a year with an extra day in it (February 29), generally occurring every 4 years EXCEPT when the year ends in 00, UNLESS that century change year is divisible by four hundred.

units.name: millennia (cal.)
units.definition: A millennium (calendar) is a unit of time equal to 1,000 years; in this case 758 years plus 242 leap years or 365,242 days.  A year is generally the time it takes for the earth to make a complete rotation around the sun.  In common usage, it refers to the length of time equal to 365 days.  A leap year is a year with an extra day in it (February 29), generally occurring every 4 years EXCEPT when the year ends in 00, UNLESS that century change year is divisible by four hundred.

units.name: millennia (sid.)
units.definition: A sidereal millenium is a unit of time defined as 1,000 sidereal years.  A sidereal year is a unit of time defined as the time elapsing between a solar eclipse of some given star and the next solar eclipse of that star.  The sidereal year lasts for 365 days, 6 hours,  9 minutes and 9.54 seconds

units.name: millennia (anom.)
units.definition: An anomalistic millennium is a unit of time defined as 1,000 anomalistic years.  An anomalistic year is defined as the time it takes for the earth to make one complete rotation around the sun.  An anomalistic year lasts for 365 days, 6 hours, 13 minutes and 53.1 seconds

units.name: barrels of beer
units.definition: A barrel is a unit of volume or capacity.  There are several types of barrels, each reflecting different fluids or solids they carry.  The "beer barrel" contains 36 imperial gallons.

units.name: gallons (Imp.)
units.definition: An imperial gallon (or British gallon) is a unit of volume defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: chaldrons (coal)
units.definition: A coal chaldron is a unit of volume equal to 36 British bushels of coal.  Its use was abolished in Britain in 1963 in favor of more standard measures of volume.

units.name: cranberry barrels
units.definition: A barrel is a unit of volume or capacity.  There are several types of barrels, each reflecting different fluids or solids they carry.  A cranberry barrel carries 5,826 cubic inches of cranberries.

units.name: barrels (Brit dry)
units.definition: A barrel is a unit of volume or capacity.  There are several types of barrels, each reflecting different fluids or solids they carry.  A British (or Imperial) barrel holds 36 British gallons, and British liquid barrels hold the same as British dry barrels.

units.name: barrels (Imperial)
units.definition: A barrel is a unit of volume or capacity.  There are several types of barrels, each reflecting different fluids or solids they carry.  An Imperial (or British) barrel holds 36 British gallons, and Imperial liquid barrels hold the same as Imperial dry barrels.

units.name: barrels (US dry)
units.definition: A barrel is a unit of volume or capacity.  There are several types of barrels, each reflecting different fluids or solids they carry.  US Dry barrels are intended for fruits, vegetables and other dry commodities, and are fixed at 7,056 cubic inches.

units.name: bushels (Winch.)
units.definition: A Winchester bushel is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 32 dry quarts.  It was much used in England from the time of Henry VIII until the imperial bushel was legally established in 1826.  It is equivalent to the US Level Bushel, which is currently used in the US.

units.name: bushels (US heap.)
units.definition: A US heaped bushel is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 2,747.715 cubic inches.  It was defined by the US Court of Customs in 1912 as a way to measure bushels of apples.

units.name: barley corns
units.definition: A barley corn is an archaic measure of length, defined early in the 12th century in England and in use for about 600 years.  A barley corn is equal to one one-third of an inch.  An inch is a unit of length, equal to one one-twelfth of a foot.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: strikes
units.definition: A strike is a unit of volume equal to two US level bushels, or two Winchester bushels.  A US level bushel is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 32 dry quarts.  It is equivalent to the Winchester bushel of 2,150.42 cubic inches, much used in England from the time of Henry VIII until the imperial bushel was legally established in 1826.

units.name: drams (Brit fl)
units.definition: A dram (or drachm) is a unit of volume equal to a little less than a teaspoon.

units.name: pounds
units.definition: A pound (or avoirdupois pound) is a unit of weight.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: ounces
units.definition: An ounce (or avoirdupois ounce) is a unit of weight equal to one one-sixteenth of a pound.  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.  The abbreviation of 'ounce' is 'oz', which derives from the Italian word 'onza', referring to the name of a Spanish and Sicilian coin.

units.name: drams
units.definition: A dram (or avoirdupois dram) is a unit of weight equal to one one-sixteenth of an ounce.  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: gallons (wine)
units.definition: A wine gallon is a British term reflecting a special gallon definition for wine.  This unit of volume was in use in the early 1700's.  A wine gallon was defined as 231 cubic inches.

units.name: bushels (corn)
units.definition: A corn bushel is a British term reflecting a special bushel definition for corn.  This unit of volume was in use in the early 1700's.  A corn bushel was defined as a circular container 18.5 inches in diameter and 8 inches deep.

units.name: gallons (corn)
units.definition: A corn gallon is a British term reflecting a special gallon definition for corn.  This unit of volume was in use in the early 1700's.  A corn gallon is equal to one one-eighth of a corn bushel, and a corn bushel was defined as a circular container 18.5 inches in diameter and 8 inches deep.

units.name: gallons (ale)
units.definition: An ale gallon is a British term reflecting a special gallon definition for ale.  This unit of volume was in use in the early 1700's.  An ale gallon was defined as 282 cubic inches.

units.name: buckets (Brit)
units.definition: A British bucket is a unit of volume equal to 4 US gallons.  A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: tons (wheat)
units.definition: A wheat ton is a unit of volume equal to 20 US bushels.  The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: tons (Brit water)
units.definition: A British water ton is a unit of volume used to measure petroleum products, and is equal to 224 British Imperial gallons.  The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: tons (seawater)
units.definition: A long ton of seawater is a unit of volume used in the past to measure a ship's displacement of seawater.  It's equal to 35 cubic feet.    The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: tons (freight)
units.definition: A freight ton a unit of volume equal to 40 cubic feet.  The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: tons (measurement)
units.definition: A measurement ton a unit of volume equal to 40 cubic feet.  The word "ton" derives from the word "tun", which was a barrel used in the wine trade.  The word tun is Old English (tunne), recorded as early as about 725; its origin is uncertain.

units.name: shekels (Heb.)
units.definition: A Hebrew shekel is a unit of weight equal to 252 wheat grains, or a coin weighing one shekel.  A grain is a small unit of weight equal to 0.065 gram, or 1/7,000 pound avoirdupois. The grain is one of the earliest units of common measure, and is a uniform unit in the avoirdupois, apothecaries', and troy systems. The defined weight of the ancient grain varied from culture to culture, but was generally defined as the weight of a designated number of dry wheat (or other edible grain) kernels taken from the middle of the ear.

units.name: shekels (Sum.)
units.definition: A Sumerian shekel is a unit of weight equal to 180 wheat grains, or a coin weighing one shekel.  A grain is a small unit of weight equal to 0.065 gram, or 1/7,000 pound avoirdupois. The grain is one of the earliest units of common measure, and is a uniform unit in the avoirdupois, apothecaries', and troy systems. The defined weight of the ancient grain varied from culture to culture, but was generally defined as the weight of a designated number of dry wheat (or other edible grain) kernels taken from the middle of the ear.

units.name: pennies (Brit sterling)
units.definition: A British silver penny sterling is a unit of weight equal to 32 wheat grains, or a coin with this weight.  A grain is a small unit of weight equal to 0.065 gram, or 1/7,000 pound avoirdupois. The grain is one of the earliest units of common measure, and is a uniform unit in the avoirdupois, apothecaries', and troy systems. The defined weight of the ancient grain varied from culture to culture, but was generally defined as the weight of a designated number of dry wheat (or other edible grain) kernels taken from the middle of the ear.

units.name: grains (metric)
units.definition: A metric grain is a unit of mass equal to 50 milligrams, and is used primarily to weight precious stones.  The metric grain should not be confused with the standard grain, weighing about 65 milligrams or 1/7,000 pound avoirdupois. The grain is one of the earliest units of common measure, and is a uniform unit in the avoirdupois, apothecaries', and troy systems. The defined weight of the ancient grain varied from culture to culture, but was generally defined as the weight of a designated number of dry wheat (or other edible grain) kernels taken from the middle of the ear.

units.name: kilderkins
units.definition: A kilderkin is a unit of volume equal to 18 British Imperial gallons.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is a unit of volume defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.  A kilderkin (sometimes spelled 'kinderkin') is also defined as half a barrel.

units.name: points (weight)
units.definition: A point is a unit of weight for diamonds and other precious gems, and is equal to one one-hundredth of a metric carat.  The metric carat was standardized in 1913 at 200 milligrams.

units.name: leagues (land)
units.definition: A land league (or statute league) is a unit of length equal to 3 miles.  A mile is a unit of length, equal to 5,280 feet.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.  In the late 18th century the league also came to be the distance a cannon shot could be fired at menacing ships offshore. This resulted in the 3-mile offshore territorial limit.

units.name: sq leagues (CA)
units.definition: A California square league is a unit of area found in old California land surveys, measuring 4,439 acres.  An acre is a unit of area equal to 10 square chains or 43,560 square feet.  A chain (Gunter's or Surveyor's) is a unit of length equal to 66 feet.

units.name: sq leagues
units.definition: A square statute league is a unit of area equal to a square measuring one statute league on a side, or 9 square miles.  A land league (or statute league) is a unit of length equal to 3 miles.  A mile is a unit of length, equal to 5,280 feet.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.

units.name: ells
units.definition: An ell is a Medieval European unit of length, equal to 45 inches, and used primarily to delineate units of wool cloth.

units.name: lasts (Brit)
units.definition: A British last is a unit of volume used to measure grain or malt, and is equal to 80 British bushels.  A British bushel is a unit of volume equal to 8 British (or Imperial) gallons.  A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water, so a last is close to three cubic meters.

units.name: lines (Brit)
units.definition: A British line is a unit of length equal to one one-twelfth of an inch.  An inch is one one-twelfth of a foot.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: miles (Brit. naut)
units.definition: A British nautical mile is a unit of length set at 6,080 feet.  It is close to the International nautical mile, defined as a unit of length equal to one minute of arc on the earth's surface at the equator or just over 6,076 feet.  A nautical mile equals about 1.15 international miles.  The word "mile" probably descended from the Roman word describing the distance equivalent to 1,000 paces.

units.name: pounds-force (avdp)
units.definition: A pound-force (using the avoirdupois pound, abbreviated as lbf) is a unit of force equal to the force a one-pound object exerts due to gravity at the surface of the earth.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: hectonewtons
units.definition: A hectonewton is a unit of force equal to 100 newtons.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  A newton is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: btu (59° F)
units.definition: A British thermal unit is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one pound of water by 1° Fahrenheit.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so British thermal units are calculated at some specified temperature (such as 59° F).

units.name: btu (39° F)
units.definition: A British thermal unit is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one pound of water by 1° Fahrenheit.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so British thermal units are calculated at some specified temperature (such as 39° F).

units.name: btu (mean)
units.definition: A British thermal unit is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one pound of water by 1° Fahrenheit.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so this "mean" British thermal unit is based on some average of initial water temperatures.

units.name: btu (th)
units.definition: The thermochemical version of the British thermal unit is a unit of energy based on the Thermochemical Calorie of 4.184 joules.

units.name: barns
units.definition: A barn is a very small unit of area equal to 1.0 e-28 square meters, used to measure the cross sections of atomic nuclei when studying interactions between the nuclei and other particles.  The physicists M. G. Holloway and C. P. Baker named it over dinner at Purdue University in December 1942.  They tried the names Oppenheimer, Bethe, Manley and John, and one author's rural background led them from John to barn.  A cross section of 10⁻²⁴ square centimeters was, for nuclear processes, "as big as a barn."  Their account does not mention the phrase "the broad side of a barn."

units.name: btu (IT)
units.definition: The International Steam Table version of the British thermal unit was defined at the 5th International Conference on the Properties of Steam, and based on the International Calorie of 4.1868 joules.  The exact conversion factor for the International Steam Table British thermal unit is 1.055 055 852 62 kilojoules.

units.name: gons
units.definition: A gon (or grade) is an angular measure reflecting the degree of inclination of a road or railroad.  It's equal to1/100th of a right angle, or 0.9 degrees, or 1/400th of a circle.

units.name: micronewtons
units.definition: A micronewton is a unit of force equal to one one-millionth of a newton.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  A newton is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: btu (60° F)
units.definition: A British thermal unit is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one pound of water by 1° Fahrenheit.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so British thermal units are calculated at some specified temperature (such as 60° F).

units.name: kilonewtons
units.definition: A kilonewton is a unit of force equal to 1,000 newtons.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  A newton is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: decinewtons
units.definition: A decinewton is a unit of force equal to one one-tenth of a newton.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  A newton is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: dekanewtons
units.definition: A dekanewton is a unit of force equal to 10 newtons.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  A newton is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: centinewtons
units.definition: A centinewton is a unit of force equal to one one-hundredth of a newton.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  A newton is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: watt-seconds
units.definition: A watt-second is the amount of work or energy expended by one watt in one second.  This energy is equivalent to one joule, or a unit of work or energy equal to the work done by a force of one newton acting through a distance of one meter.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  This force is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: tons-force
units.definition: A ton-force is a unit of force equal to 2,000 lbf.  A pound-force (using the avoirdupois pound, abbreviated as lbf) is a unit of force equal to the force a one-pound object exerts due to gravity at the surface of the earth.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: ounces-force
units.definition: An ounce-force (abbreviated as ozf) is a unit of force equal to 1/16 lbf.  A pound-force (using the avoirdupois pound, abbreviated as lbf) is a unit of force equal to the force a one-pound object exerts due to gravity at the surface of the earth.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.  The abbreviation of 'ounce' is 'oz', which derives from the Italian word 'onza', referring to the name of a Spanish and Sicilian coin.

units.name: kips
units.definition: A kip is a unit of force equal to 1,000 lbf.  A pound-force (using the avoirdupois pound, abbreviated as lbf) is a unit of force equal to the force a one-pound object exerts due to gravity at the surface of the earth.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: kiloponds
units.definition: A kilopond (abbreviated as kp), or kilogram-force (abbreviated as kbf) is a unit of force equal to the force a one-kilogram object exerts due to gravity at the surface of the earth.  A kilogram is a unit of mass equal to 1,000 grams.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: kilograms-force
units.definition: A kilogram-force (abbreviated as kbf), or kilopond (abbreviated as kp) is a unit of force equal to the force a one-kilogram object exerts due to gravity at the surface of the earth.  A kilogram is a unit of mass equal to 1,000 grams.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.

units.name: meganewtons
units.definition: A meganewton is a unit of force equal to 1,000,000 newtons.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  A newton is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: kilocalories (IT)
units.definition: An International Steam Table kilocalorie is a unit of energy equal to 1,000 calories.  A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature.  Because of the problems with different water temperatures, the "International Steam Table calorie" is defined to be exactly equal to 4.1868 joules.

units.name: calories (IT)
units.definition: A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature.  Because of the problems with different water temperatures, the "International Steam Table calorie" is defined to be exactly equal to 4.1868 joules.

units.name: watt-hours (abs)
units.definition: A watt-hour is the amount of work or energy expended by one watt in one hour.

units.name: tons of TNT
units.definition: A ton of TNT, in this case, is a large unit of energy defined as 4,814,000,000 joules.  This is just a defined value.  Nobody actually measured the exact energy output of a ton of TNT.

units.name: therms (U.S.)
units.definition: A therm (U.S.) is a unit of energy equal to 1.054804 e+8 joules.  The therm (U.S.) is legally defined in the Federal Register of July 27, 1968 and is used by the U.S. natural gas industry.  Interestingly, engineers in the United States often use the therm (EC), which is based on the British thermal unit.

units.name: therms (EC)
units.definition: A therm (EC) is a unit of energy equal to 1.05506 e+8 joules.  The therm (EC) is legally defined in the Council Directive of 20 December 1979, Council of the European Communities (now the European Union, EU).  Interestingly, engineers in the United States often use the therm (EC) while the US natural gas industry uses the therm (U.S.).

units.name: quads
units.definition: A quad is a unit of energy equal to one quadrillion International Steam Table British thermal units.  The International Steam Table version of the British thermal unit was defined at the 5th International Conference on the Properties of Steam, and based on the International Calorie of 4.1868 joules.  The exact conversion factor for the International Steam Table British thermal unit is 1.055 055 852 62 kilojoules.

units.name: kilowatt-hours
units.definition: A kilowatt-hour is the amount of work or energy expended by one kilowatt in one hour.

units.name: kilocalories (mean)
units.definition: A kilocalorie is equal to 1,000 calories.  A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so this "mean" kilocalorie reflects some average of initial water temperatures.

units.name: millinewtons
units.definition: A millinewton is a unit of force equal to one one-thousandth of a newton.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  A newton is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: kilocalories (th)
units.definition: A thermochemical kilocalorie is equal to 1,000 thermochemical calories.  A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature.  Because of the problems with different water temperatures, the "thermochemical calorie" was defined to be exactly equal to 4.184 joules.

units.name: calorie kgs (IT-nut.)
units.definition: The kilogram calorie (or large calorie) is a unit of energy used to describe the energy content of foods.  The term kilogram calorie is an obsolete term for the kilocalorie, and the "kilo" prefix is often omitted when discussing foods.  A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature.  Because of the problems with different water temperatures, the "International Steam Table calorie" is defined to be exactly equal to 4.1868 joules.

units.name: calories (th)
units.definition: A calorie (or gram calorie, or small calorie) is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature.  Because of the problems with different water temperatures, the "thermochemical calorie" was defined to be exactly equal to 4.184 joules.

units.name: calories (mean)
units.definition: A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so this "mean" calorie reflects some average of initial water temperatures.

units.name: calories (20° C)
units.definition: A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature (such as 20° C).

units.name: foot-pounds
units.definition: A foot-pound (ft-lb), or pound-force foot, is the amount of work required to raise a mass of 1 pound through an elevation of 1 foot at sea level and 45° latitude.

units.name: calorie kgs (th-nut.)
units.definition: The kilogram calorie (or large calorie) is a unit of energy used to describe the energy content of foods.  The term kilogram calorie is an obsolete term for the kilocalorie, and the "kilo" prefix is often omitted when discussing foods.  A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature.  Because of the problems with different water temperatures, the "thermochemical calorie" was defined to be exactly equal to 4.184 joules.

units.name: calorie kgs (mean)
units.definition: The kilogram calorie (or large calorie) is a unit of energy used to describe the energy content of foods.  The term kilogram calorie is an obsolete term for the kilocalorie, and the "kilo" prefix is often omitted when discussing foods.  A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so this "mean" kilocalorie reflects some average of initial water temperatures.

units.name: electron-volts
units.definition: An electron-volt is equal to the energy of one electron accelerated by one volt. Exact since the 2019 redefinition of the SI, which fixed the charge of the electron: 1.602176634 x 10^-19 joule.

units.name: ergs
units.definition: An erg is a unit of energy equal to the amount of work expended moving 1 dyne through 1 centimeter of space, or 1.0 e-7 joules.  A dyne is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second system equal to the force that would give a free mass of one gram an acceleration of one centimeter per second squared.  This force translates to a weight of about .001 grams on the surface of the earth.

units.name: foot-poundals
units.definition: A foot-poundal is the amount of work required to raise a mass of 1 poundal through an elevation of 1 foot at sea level and 45° latitude.  A poundal is a unit of force in the foot-pound-second system, and is a unit of force equal to the force that would give a free mass of one pound an acceleration of one foot per second squared.  This force is equal to a weight of .031 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: calories (15° C)
units.definition: A calorie is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature (such as 15° C).

units.name: calories (small)
units.definition: A calorie (or gram calorie, or small calorie) is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature.  Because of the problems with different water temperatures, the "thermochemical calorie" was defined to be exactly equal to 4.184 joules.

units.name: calories (gram)
units.definition: A calorie (or gram calorie, or small calorie) is defined as approximately the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1° Celsius.  This definition is dependent on the initial temperature of the water, however, and so calories are sometimes calculated at some specified temperature.  Because of the problems with different water temperatures, the "thermochemical calorie" was defined to be exactly equal to 4.184 joules.

units.name: joules
units.definition: A joule is a unit of work or energy equal to the work done by one volt acting through a resistance of one ohm for one second, and this is slightly more than the International Steam Table joule, which equals a force of one newton acting through a distance of one meter.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  This force is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: joules (Int)
units.definition: An international joule (Int) is a unit of work or energy from the international electrical units in use before the present SI units, equal to 1.000165 joules (CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 62nd edition).

units.name: dyne-cm
units.definition: An dyne-centimeter (or erg) is a unit of energy equal to the amount of work expended moving 1 dyne through 1 centimeter of space, or 1.0 e-7 joules.  A dyne is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second system equal to the force that would give a free mass of one gram an acceleration of one centimeter per second squared.  This force translates to a weight of about .001 grams on the surface of the earth.

units.name: watt-seconds (Int)
units.definition: A watt-second (Int) is a unit of work or energy equal to a international joule, or slightly more than a standard joule.  A joule is a unit of work or energy equal to the work done by a force of one newton acting through a distance of one meter.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  This force is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: volt-coulombs (Int)
units.definition: An volt-coulomb (Int) is a unit of work or energy equal to a international joule, or slightly more than a standard joule.  A joule is a unit of work or energy equal to the work done by a force of one newton acting through a distance of one meter.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  This force is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: volt-coulombs
units.definition: A volt-coulomb is a unit of work or energy equal to a joule, or the work done by one volt acting through a resistance of one ohm for one second, and is slightly more than the International Steam Table joule, which equals a force of one newton acting through a distance of one meter.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  This force is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: horsepower-hrs
units.definition: A horsepower-hour is a unit of energy equal to the amount of work expended by one horsepower working for one hour.  A horsepower was originally defined as the power necessary to lift 33,000 pounds a distance of one foot in one minute, and was based on the strength of strong Scottish dray horses.  This calculated value is actually about 50% higher than the rate of work an average horse can sustain for a day.

units.name: gram-cm
units.definition: An gram-centimeter is a unit of energy equal to the amount of work expended moving 1 gram through 1 centimeter of space.

units.name: tons, assay
units.definition: An assay ton is a unit of weight equal to a little over 29 grams.  A gram is a unit of mass nearly equal to one cubic centimeter of water at the temperature of it's maximum density.  The assay ton is a unit of mass used to estimate the amount of precious metals in a ton of ore.  The number of milligrams of precious metal in an assay ton of ore corresponds to the number of troy ounces of precious metal in 2,000 pounds of that ore.

units.name: newton-meters
units.definition: A newton-meter (or joule) is a unit of work or energy equal to the work done by a force of one newton acting through a distance of one meter.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  This force is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: inch-pounds
units.definition: An inch-pound (in-lb), or pound-force inch, is the amount of work required to raise a mass of 1 pound through an elevation of 1 inch at sea level and 45° latitude.

units.name: kg-meters
units.definition: An kilogram-meter is a unit of energy equal to the amount of work expended moving 1 kilogram through 1 meter of space.

units.name: oz-inches
units.definition: An ounce-force inch (avoirdupois ounce) is a unit of energy equal to the amount of work expended moving 1 ounce (avoirdupois) through 1 inch of space.

units.name: acre-lengths
units.definition: An acre-length is a unit of length equal to 660 feet, derived from an early English definition of an acre.  An acre is a unit of area equal to 10 square chains or 43,560 square feet.  An acre was originally defined as the amount of land that a yoke of oxen could plough in a day, and eventually redefined as an area equal to "40 poles long by 4 broad," or 32 furrow-lengths.  "40 poles long" equals one acre-length.

units.name: acre-breadths
units.definition: An acre-breadth is a unit of length equal to 66 feet, derived from an early English definition of an acre.  An acre is a unit of area equal to 10 square chains or 43,560 square feet.  An acre was originally defined as the amount of land that a yoke of oxen could plough in a day, and eventually redefined as an area equal to "40 poles long by 4 broad," or 32 furrow-lengths.  "4 poles broad" equals one acre-breadth.

units.name: pipes
units.definition: A pipe is a unit of volume or capacity equal to 126 US liquid gallons.  The term refers to a cask for wine, beer, fish, cider, beef, etc. and equal to half a tun, or 2 hogsheads, or 126 wine-gallons (equivalent to 126 US Liquid gallons).

The term 'cord' is probably derived from an early way to measure it, by stretching a cord of fixed length around it.

units.name: diameters
units.definition: A diameter is a unit of length, reflecting the length of a line passing from one side of a circle to the other, and passing through the center.  One diameter is equal to two radians, and a full circle is equal to PI diameters.

units.name: degrees Centigrade

The term 'centigrade' is rarely used these days in favor of 'Celsius', the name of the inventor of the scale.

units.name: microinches

units.name: cu. foot-atms

units.name: cu. m. gas eqv.

A therm (U.S.) is a unit of energy equal to 1.054804 e+8 joules.  The therm (U.S.) is legally defined in the Federal Register of July 27, 1968 and is used by the U.S. natural gas industry.  Interestingly, engineers in the United States often use the therm (EC), which is based on the British thermal unit.

units.name: volt-coul. / sec
units.definition: A volt-coulomb per second is a unit of power defined as the power output produced by energy being applied at the rate of one volt-coulomb per second.  A volt-coulomb is a unit of work or energy equal to a joule, or the work done by one volt acting through a resistance of one ohm for one second, and is slightly more than the International Steam Table joule, which equals a force of one newton acting through a distance of one meter.  A newton is a unit of force in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kilogram object at a rate of 1 meter per second per second.  This force is equivalent to about .2248 pounds on the surface of the earth.

units.name: cu. feet / min
units.definition: A cubic foot per minute is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one cubic foot per minute.  A cubic foot is a unit of volume equal to a cube measuring 1 foot on a side.  A foot is a unit of length, originally based on the length of the human foot.

units.name: gall. (US) / min
units.definition: A US liquid gallon per minute is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one US liquid gallon per minute. A gallon is a unit of volume.  The word comes from the Old Northern French galon, related to the medieval Latin galleta, a measure for wine.

units.name: liters / min
units.definition: A liter per minute is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one liter per minute. A liter (or litre) is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter, although according to the Oxford English Dictionary (citing the Physics Bull. Feb. 58/2, 1969),  "It was a regrettable international decision in 1964 which reinstated the name litre for a cubic decimetre".  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

A British gallon (or Imperial gallon) is a unit of volume defined as the space occupied by 10 pounds of distilled water with a density of 0.998859 grams per millilitre.

units.name: kips / sq. in
units.definition: A kip per square inch is a unit of pressure defined as a force of one kip concentrated on a square inch of surface area.  A kip is a unit of force equal to 1,000 lbf.  A pound-force (using the avoirdupois pound, abbreviated as lbf) is a unit of force equal to the force a one-pound object exerts due to gravity at the surface of the earth.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

The term 'bar' is short for 'barometer.'

units.name: mmHg (conv.)

A standard atmosphere is equal to 760 millimeters of mercury.  According to the Guide for the International System of Units (see Sources), "Conversion factors for mercury [and water] manometer pressure units are calculated using the standard value for the acceleration of gravity and the density of mercury at the stated temperature.  Additional digits [beyond 7 significant digits] are not justified because the definitions of the units do not take into account the compressibility of mercury [or water] or the change in density caused by the revised practical temperature scale, ITS-90."

A pascal is a unit of pressure in the metre-kilogram-second (SI) system named after French mathematician and physicist Blaise Pascal (1623-1662), and defined as a pressure of one newton concentrated on one square meter.

units.name: ft H2O (60° F)
units.definition: A barometric foot of water, in this case, is a unit of pressure defined as the atmospheric pressure necessary to balance a column of water one foot high, with the water temperature equal to 60° F.  According to the Guide for the International System of Units (see Sources), "Conversion factors for mercury [and water] manometer pressure units are calculated using the standard value for the acceleration of gravity and the density of mercury at the stated temperature.  Additional digits [beyond 7 significant digits] are not justified because the definitions of the units do not take into account the compressibility of mercury [or water] or the change in density caused by the revised practical temperature scale, ITS-90."

units.name: m H2O (4° C)
units.definition: A barometric meter of water, in this case, is a unit of pressure defined as the atmospheric pressure necessary to balance a column of water one meter high, with the water temperature equal to 4° C.  According to the Guide for the International System of Units (see Sources), "Conversion factors for mercury [and water] manometer pressure units are calculated using the standard value for the acceleration of gravity and the density of mercury at the stated temperature.  Additional digits [beyond 7 significant digits] are not justified because the definitions of the units do not take into account the compressibility of mercury [or water] or the change in density caused by the revised practical temperature scale, ITS-90."

units.name: m H2O (conv.)
units.definition: A conventional barometric meter of water is a unit of pressure defined as the atmospheric pressure necessary to balance a column of water one meter high.  A standard atmosphere is equal to a little more than 10 meters of water.  According to the Guide for the International System of Units (see Sources), "Conversion factors for mercury [and water] manometer pressure units are calculated using the standard value for the acceleration of gravity and the density of mercury at the stated temperature.  Additional digits [beyond 7 significant digits] are not justified because the definitions of the units do not take into account the compressibility of mercury [or water] or the change in density caused by the revised practical temperature scale, ITS-90."

units.name: tons / sq. foot
units.definition: A ton per square foot is a unit of pressure defined as one ton of weight concentrated on one square foot of surface area.

units.name: tons / sq. inch
units.definition: A ton per square inch is a unit of pressure defined as one ton of weight concentrated on one square inch of surface area.

units.name: amu (chem.)
units.definition: An atomic mass unit (or 'amu', also expressed as a 'dalton') is a unit of mass used to calculate the quantity of mass contained in an atom, and defined as one one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.  In this case, the value for an atomic mass unit is derived using chemical measurement methods rather than physical methods.

units.name: amu (phys.)
units.definition: An atomic mass unit (or 'amu', also expressed as a 'dalton') is a unit of mass used to calculate the quantity of mass contained in an atom, and defined as one one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.  In this case, the value for an atomic mass unit is derived using physical measurement methods rather than chemical ones.

units.name: barrels (wine)
units.definition: A barrel is a unit of volume or capacity.  There are several types of barrels, each reflecting different fluids or solids they carry.  The wine barrel contains 31.5 wine gallons, equivalent to 31.5 US liquid gallons.

units.name: kips / sq. ft
units.definition: A kip per square foot is a unit of pressure defined as a force of one kip concentrated on a square inch of surface area.  A kip is a unit of force equal to 1,000 lbf.  A pound-force (using the avoirdupois pound, abbreviated as lbf) is a unit of force equal to the force a one-pound object exerts due to gravity at the surface of the earth.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: kips / sq. yd
units.definition: A kip per square yard is a unit of pressure defined as a force of one kip concentrated on a square inch of surface area.  A kip is a unit of force equal to 1,000 lbf.  A pound-force (using the avoirdupois pound, abbreviated as lbf) is a unit of force equal to the force a one-pound object exerts due to gravity at the surface of the earth.  The abbreviation (lb) descends from the Roman weight "Libra."  The avoirdupois system of weights probably originated during the Medieval trade fairs held in the former French province of Champagne, in the 12th and 13th centuries, and is still in use today in places that haven't switched to the metric system.  The name comes from the Anglo-Norman and Old French avoir de pois (pois, weight), which in English first meant merchandise sold by weight.

units.name: tons / sq. yd
units.definition: A ton per square foot is a unit of pressure defined as one ton of weight concentrated on one square foot of surface area.

units.name: megaliters / sec
units.definition: A megaliter per second is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one megaliter per second.  A megaliter is a unit of volume equal to 1,000,000 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: megaliters / min
units.definition: A megaliter per minute is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one megaliter per minute.  A megaliter is a unit of volume equal to 1,000,000 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: megaliters / hr
units.definition: A megaliter per hour is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one megaliter per hour.  A megaliter is a unit of volume equal to 1,000,000 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: megaliters / day
units.definition: A megaliter per day is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one megaliter per day.  A megaliter is a unit of volume equal to 1,000,000 liters.  A liter is a unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter.  A decimeter is one tenth of a meter.  A meter is a unit of length defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.  One meter translates into slightly longer than three feet.

units.name: megasteres / sec
units.definition: A megastere per second is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one megastere per second.  A megastere is a unit of volume equal to 1,000,000 steres, or 1,000,000 cubic meters.

units.name: megasteres / min
units.definition: A megastere per minute is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one megastere per minute.  A megastere is a unit of volume equal to 1,000,000 steres, or 1,000,000 cubic meters.

units.name: megasteres / hr
units.definition: A megastere per hour is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one megastere per hour.  A megastere is a unit of volume equal to 1,000,000 steres, or 1,000,000 cubic meters.

units.name: megasteres / day
units.definition: A megastere per day is a unit of flow, or of volume divided by time, equal to some substance (usually a liquid) passing a point at the rate of one megastere per day.  A megastere is a unit of volume equal to 1,000,000 steres, or 1,000,000 cubic meters.

units.name: inches (US survey)
units.definition: A U.S. survey inch is a unit of length equal to one twelfth of a U.S. survey foot, or 100/3937 meter. ArcGIS Pro calls it Inch_US. The U.S. survey foot was retired by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the National Geodetic Survey at the end of 2022; since then, U.S. measurements use the international foot of exactly 0.3048 meter. This unit is kept for older surveys and records.

units.name: animal unit months
units.definition: An animal unit month (AUM) is the amount of forage one animal unit eats in one month, the usual measure of grazing use and carrying capacity. The animal unit is a 1,000-pound cow with a calf 6 months old or younger by her side; an animal unit month (AUM) is the forage it needs for one month. The Bureau of Land Management's grazing regulations define it as the forage needed to sustain one cow or its equivalent for 1 month.

units.name: animal unit days
units.definition: An animal unit day (AUD) is the forage one animal unit eats in one day. The NRCS handbook's animal unit year is both 12 animal unit months and 365 animal unit days (9,490 pounds of oven-dry forage at 26 pounds a day), so a month here is 365/12 = 30.42 days. The Society for Range Management's glossary counts 30 animal unit days in an AUM instead. The animal unit is a 1,000-pound cow with a calf 6 months old or younger by her side; an animal unit month (AUM) is the forage it needs for one month.

units.name: animal unit years
units.definition: An animal unit year (AUY) is the forage one animal unit eats in a year, 12 animal unit months. The animal unit is a 1,000-pound cow with a calf 6 months old or younger by her side; an animal unit month (AUM) is the forage it needs for one month.

units.name: head months (federal grazing fees)
units.definition: A head month, the unit of federal grazing fees: one month's grazing by one cow, bull, steer, heifer, horse, burro or mule over 6 months old or weaned (Bureau of Land Management, 43 CFR 4130.8-1), or by one animal other than a sheep or goat (Forest Service, 36 CFR 222.50). The two agencies treat a head month and an AUM as the same measure for fees. It counts head, not forage: a bull or a horse counts as 1 here, where the NDSU equivalents count 1.40 and 1.25.

units.name: sheep or goat months (federal grazing fees)
units.singular: sheep or goat month (federal grazing fees)
units.definition: One month's grazing by one sheep or goat, for federal grazing fees: five sheep or five goats count as one head month or AUM (43 CFR 4130.8-1; 36 CFR 222.50). The NDSU equivalents count a mature goat as 0.15 and a mature sheep with lamb as 0.20.

units.name: pounds of air-dried forage (913 lb/AUM)

Agencies and regions use different amounts; choose the one your agency uses.

units.name: kilograms of oven-dry forage (780 lb/AUM)
units.definition: Kilograms of oven-dry forage, counted in animal unit months at 780 pounds (353.8 kilograms) per AUM. The Society for Range Management's glossary counts 26 pounds of oven-dry forage a day for a standardized month of 30 animal unit days, 780 pounds.

units.name: pounds of air-dried forage (750 lb/AUM)
units.definition: Pounds of air-dried forage, counted in animal unit months at 750 pounds per AUM. University of Wyoming Extension B-1320 (2018) uses 750 pounds of air-dried forage per AUM: a 1,000-pound cow eating 2.5 percent of her weight a day for 30 days. Agencies and regions use different amounts; choose the one your agency uses.

units.name: kilograms of air-dried forage (750 lb/AUM)
